Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

SAN DIEGO, California (CNN) -- On the question of whether recent immigrants assimilate as quickly as previous waves, many Americans exhibit short fuses -- and even shorter memories. Ruben Navarrette Jr. notes that immigrants have been criticized throughout history for not assimilating. They have convinced themselves that, instead of adapting to the customs of this country, new arrivals -- most of whom come from Asia or Latin America -- expect the rest of us to accommodate them. They go ballistic over little things -- Mexican flags, taco trucks, libraries that offer bilingual story time, or having to "press one for English." Yet, even as they look down on new immigrants, many Americans look back fondly upon their immigrant ancestors. Legend has it that when grandpa arrived from Ireland, Germany, Italy or Poland, he jumped off the boat, immediately draped himself in the American flag, ripped out his native tongue, and abandoned his culture -- all while singing "Yankee Doodle Dandy." Germans did not move to Milwaukee and make beer and cheese. The Irish did not settle in Boston and join organizations like the Hibernian Society to preserve their heritage and culture. And even while Americans complain about how the current crop of immigrants aren't like their predecessors, they miss the irony: At the time, there were people who said the same thing about their ancestors; the Germans were thought to not be like the English, the Irish weren't like the Germans, the Italians weren't like the Irish etc. And the Chinese weren't like anyone who had come before them, and so they were labeled "unassimilable" by the Tom Tancredos of that era. Some things never change. When I was growing up in Central California, which is home to a large population of immigrants from Southeast Asia, thousands would gather to celebrate Hmong New Year. The local newspaper would do a feature. And, in the days that followed, someone would write an angry letter to the editor complaining that these people weren't melting into the pot. Yet, there is more melting going on than one might think, according to a new report from the Manhattan Institute. Billed as the first annual Index of Immigrant Assimilation, the study was written by Duke University Professor Jacob Vigdor. It measured three kinds of assimilation: economic (employment, education, homeownership, etc.); cultural (intermarriage, English proficiency, family size, etc.); and civic (citizenship, military service, political participation, etc.). Far from discovering that recent immigrants are ducking the assimilation process, the study found that "immigrants of the past quarter-century have assimilated more rapidly than their counterparts of a century ago, even though they are more distinct from the native population upon arrival." Of course, individual groups still fall behind in some categories. Chinese and Indian immigrants have low levels of cultural assimilation. Mexican immigrants have low levels of economic assimilation. And Canadian and Indian immigrants have low levels of civic assimilation, since few of them become citizens. But, overall, the news is good. After more than 200 years, America still does an excellent job of assimilating immigrants. Even if a particular group tried to resist the process, they wouldn't stand a chance. Assimilation happens, whether the immigrants are ready or not. Those are the facts. Of course, fear doesn't listen to facts. That is something else that hasn't changed. Ruben Navarrette Jr. is a member of the editorial board of the San Diego Union-Tribune and a nationally syndicated columnist. Read his column here. The opinions expressed in this commentary are solely those of the writer.

Never mind that Germans settled in Milwaukee and continued brewing beer and making cheese, or that the Irish established roots in Boston and formed organizations like the Hibernian Society specifically to preserve their heritage.

What's more, as Americans lament how today's immigrants differ from their predecessors, they overlook a striking irony: people made the very same complaints about earlier generations. The Germans were considered unlike the English; the Irish, unlike the Germans; the Italians, unlike the Irish. The Chinese, meanwhile, were unlike anyone who had come before, earning them the label "unassimilable" from the Tom Tancredos of that era. Some things, it seems, never change.

Growing up in Central California—home to a substantial population of immigrants from Southeast Asia—I witnessed thousands gather each year to celebrate Hmong New Year. The local newspaper would run a feature on the festivities, and inevitably, in the days that followed, someone would fire off an angry letter to the editor complaining that these newcomers weren't melting into the pot.

Yet more melting is occurring than many might assume, according to a new report from the Manhattan Institute. Billed as the first annual Index of Immigrant Assimilation, the study—authored by Duke University Professor Jacob Vigdor—measured three dimensions of assimilation: economic (employment, education, homeownership, and the like); cultural (intermarriage, English proficiency, family size, and so forth); and civic (citizenship, military service, political participation, among other factors).

Far from confirming that recent immigrants are shirking the assimilation process, the study found that "immigrants of the past quarter-century have assimilated more rapidly than their counterparts of a century ago, even though they are more distinct from the native population upon arrival."

Naturally, individual groups still lag in certain categories. Chinese and Indian immigrants show comparatively low levels of cultural assimilation. Mexican immigrants demonstrate low levels of economic assimilation. And both Canadian and Indian immigrants exhibit low levels of civic assimilation, given that relatively few pursue citizenship.

On the whole, however, the news is encouraging. After more than two centuries, America continues to excel at assimilating immigrants. Even when a particular group resists the process, it stands little chance of succeeding indefinitely—assimilation happens, whether immigrants are ready for it or not.

These are the facts. Fear, of course, has never listened to facts. That, too, remains unchanged.

# Immigration Debate: History Repeats Itself, But Facts Tell a Different Story

*By CNN Commentary*

When it comes to whether today's newcomers integrate into American society as effectively as those who came before them, plenty of Americans react with anger and conveniently selective memory. Columnist Ruben Navarrette Jr. points out that this criticism isn't new—every generation of immigrants has faced accusations of failing to assimilate.

The prevailing belief seems to be that rather than adjusting to American norms, today's arrivals—predominantly from Latin America and Asia—demand that everyone else bend to accommodate them instead. Minor cultural expressions trigger outsized outrage: a Mexican flag displayed somewhere, a taco truck parked on a corner, a library hosting bilingual storytime, or the simple instruction to "press one for English."

Ironically, while criticizing new immigrants, many of these same Americans romanticize their own immigrant heritage. Family lore suggests that great-grandpa, upon stepping off the boat from Poland, Italy, Germany, or Ireland, instantly wrapped himself in American symbolism, dropped his native language, and shed his cultural identity entirely—presumably while humming patriotic tunes.

The reality tells a different story. German immigrants didn't establish beer and cheese traditions in Milwaukee. Irish immigrants didn't form heritage organizations like the Hibernian Society in Boston to preserve their traditions. History conveniently gets rewritten.

What's particularly ironic is that Americans complaining about current immigrants failing to match previous generations are unknowingly echoing exactly what people said about *those* generations. The English viewed Germans with suspicion; Germans looked down on the Irish; the Irish, in turn, criticized Italians. Chinese immigrants faced the harshest judgment of all, branded "unassimilable" by nativist voices of that era—essentially the historical equivalent of today's immigration hardliners. The pattern repeats endlessly.

## A Personal Observation

Growing up in California's Central Valley—an area with a substantial Southeast Asian immigrant population—Navarrette recalls annual Hmong New Year celebrations drawing thousands of attendees. Local media would cover the festivities, and predictably, letters to the editor would follow, criticizing these communities for supposedly refusing to blend into mainstream American culture.

## What the Data Actually Shows

Contrary to popular perception, recent research suggests far more integration is occurring than commonly assumed. The Manhattan Institute's inaugural Immigrant Assimilation Index, authored by Duke University's Professor Jacob Vigdor, examined three dimensions of integration:

- **Economic** — measures like employment rates, educational attainment, and homeownership
- **Cultural** — factors including intermarriage rates, English fluency, and family size
- **Civic** — indicators such as citizenship status, military participation, and political engagement

Rather than confirming fears that modern immigrants avoid integrating, the research revealed the opposite: today's immigrants are assimilating *faster* than those who arrived a century ago—despite starting from a position of greater cultural difference from native-born Americans.

Certain patterns did emerge within specific groups. Chinese and Indian immigrants showed weaker cultural integration scores. Mexican immigrants lagged in economic assimilation metrics. Canadian and Indian populations demonstrated lower civic integration, largely due to lower citizenship rates.

## The Bottom Line

Despite these variations, the overall picture remains encouraging. More than two centuries into the American experiment, the country continues to successfully absorb newcomers into its social fabric. Integration happens organically over time—regardless of whether immigrant communities actively resist the process or not.

The data speaks clearly. But as history demonstrates, fear rarely bothers to listen to facts. That, apparently, is one thing that never changes.

*Ruben Navarrette Jr. serves on the editorial board of the San Diego Union-Tribune and writes a nationally syndicated column. The views expressed here belong solely to the author.*

# The Recurring Myth of Immigrant Assimilation

Ruben Navarrette Jr. presents a compelling argument that the criticism immigrants face for failing to assimilate into American culture is not a new phenomenon unique to contemporary debates about immigration—rather, it represents a recurring pattern that has played out repeatedly throughout the nation's history. This perspective challenges a comfortable narrative that many Americans have constructed about their own family histories.

## The Selective Memory of Assimilation

Many Americans harbor a nostalgic and largely inaccurate view of how their own immigrant ancestors integrated into American society. There exists a popular belief that previous generations of immigrants arrived on American shores and immediately, almost magically, shed their native languages, customs, and cultural identities in favor of complete Americanization. This romanticized version of history suggests a clean, swift transition from "foreign" to "American" that simply does not align with the historical record. In reality, the process of cultural integration has always been gradual, complex, and multigenerational—not the instantaneous transformation that nostalgia often implies.

## Historical Evidence of Cultural Persistence

The historical record tells a very different story than the one commonly remembered. Various ethnic groups who immigrated to America in earlier centuries actively worked to preserve their cultural heritage rather than abandoning it wholesale. German immigrants, for instance, established breweries that not only provided economic opportunity but also served as cultural institutions reflecting their homeland traditions. Irish immigrants formed heritage societies and maintained strong communal bonds that preserved their distinct cultural identity for generations. Italian immigrants similarly created neighborhoods, organizations, and traditions that kept their cultural practices alive well beyond the first generation. These examples demonstrate that maintaining connections to one's heritage while simultaneously building a life in America has always been the norm, not the exception.

## The Irony of Historical Amnesia

Perhaps the most striking aspect of this pattern is its cyclical, almost predictable nature. Each wave of immigrants arriving in America faced criticism from those who had arrived before them, with earlier immigrants often being the harshest critics of newer arrivals. Germans faced skepticism about their ability to assimilate, only for German communities to later question the assimilation of Irish immigrants. The Irish, once targets of such criticism themselves, would later express similar doubts about Italian immigrants. This pattern continued with Chinese immigrants facing comparable accusations. This recurring irony reveals a troubling historical amnesia—each generation seems to forget that their own ancestors faced identical criticisms, allowing the same unfounded concerns to resurface with each new immigrant population.

## A Personal Witness to the Pattern

The author brings this historical pattern into sharp, personal focus through a firsthand account from childhood in Central California. Growing up in this region, the author observed Hmong New Year celebrations that served as vital expressions of cultural heritage and community identity for Hmong immigrants. Despite these celebrations being a perfectly natural and healthy way for an immigrant community to honor its traditions while building a new life in America, they drew criticism from other community members. This personal observation serves as a microcosm of the larger historical pattern, illustrating how the same tensions and misunderstandings that characterized earlier waves of immigration continue to manifest in contemporary communities—proving that the cycle of criticism directed at cultural preservation among immigrants remains very much alive today.

# The Recurring Myth of the "Unassimilable" Immigrant

Every generation seems to rediscover the same anxiety: that the immigrants arriving today are somehow different from those who came before—less willing to learn English, less eager to embrace American values, more insistent on clinging to the customs of the old country. This complaint feels urgent and unprecedented to those who voice it. Yet, as columnist Ruben Navarrette Jr. persuasively argues, this fear is not a new phenomenon responding to a genuinely new threat. Instead, it is a script that America has performed repeatedly throughout its history, with only the cast of characters changing.

Navarrette traces this pattern back through successive waves of American immigration. In the nineteenth century, German immigrants were viewed with suspicion for maintaining their own language, publishing German-language newspapers, and forming insular communities that seemed resistant to Anglo-American culture. Following closely behind, Irish immigrants faced intense nativist hostility—not only for their Catholic faith, which many Protestant Americans viewed as fundamentally incompatible with democratic values, but also for their perceived clannishness and reluctance to shed their distinct cultural identity. Italian immigrants encountered similar accusations decades later, stereotyped as insular, criminal, and unwilling to fully embrace American norms. Chinese immigrants, meanwhile, faced not just cultural criticism but outright legal exclusion, codified in the Chinese Exclusion Act, based on the belief that they were fundamentally unassimilable due to racial and cultural differences too vast to bridge.

What makes this historical pattern so revealing, according to Navarrette, is how completely each of these groups eventually became woven into the fabric of American identity. Germans, Irish, and Italians are now considered quintessentially American, their descendants rarely giving a second thought to the suspicion their ancestors once faced. Their languages faded into English within a generation or two, their religious and cultural practices blended into the broader American mosaic, and the very idea that they once represented a threat to national cohesion now seems almost absurd.

This is precisely why Navarrette finds the current wave of anxiety—directed now at Asian and Latin American immigrants—so ironic. The same accusations are being recycled: that these newcomers refuse to learn English, that they maintain excessive loyalty to their countries of origin, that their cultural practices are too foreign to ever truly integrate into American society. These claims echo almost word-for-word the criticisms once leveled at Germans, Irish, Italians, and Chinese immigrants.

The deeper insight here is that this cyclical criticism reveals more about collective forgetting than about any genuine difference in immigrant behavior. Each generation of native-born Americans seems to forget that their own ancestors faced identical accusations, allowing them to view current immigrants as uniquely resistant to assimilation rather than recognizing the pattern for what it is: a recurring social anxiety that surfaces whenever a new, visibly different group arrives in significant numbers. The "evidence" cited as proof of failure to assimilate—maintaining native languages at home, preserving cultural or religious traditions, forming communities with others who share a similar background—was true of every previous immigrant group as well, and yet assimilation ultimately occurred, just as it does today, often within a single generation.

In this light, Navarrette suggests that the real story is not one of immigrants failing to adapt, but of a society with a persistently short historical memory, prone to viewing each new wave of arrivals through the same lens of suspicion its own ancestors once endured.

# San Diego: America's Finest City

San Diego, California, is a vibrant coastal city located in the southern part of the state, just north of the border with Mexico. Known for its perfect year-round climate, stunning beaches, and laid-back atmosphere, San Diego has earned the nickname "America's Finest City."

## History and Founding

San Diego holds the distinction of being the birthplace of California, as it was the site of the first European settlement in the state. In 1769, Spanish explorers established a mission and presidio here, marking the beginning of European colonization in California. This rich history is still visible today in areas like Old Town San Diego, which preserves the city's early architecture and cultural heritage.

## Geography and Climate

Situated along the Pacific Ocean, San Diego boasts approximately 70 miles of coastline, featuring some of the most beautiful beaches in the country, including La Jolla Cove, Pacific Beach, and Coronado. The city enjoys a Mediterranean climate with mild temperatures throughout the year, rarely dipping below 50°F (10°C) or rising above 80°F (27°C), making it an ideal destination for outdoor enthusiasts.

## Economy and Attractions

San Diego's economy is diverse, driven by several key industries:

- **Military and Defense**: Home to numerous naval installations, including Naval Base San Diego
- **Tourism**: Millions of visitors flock to attractions like the world-famous San Diego Zoo and SeaWorld
- **Biotechnology and Research**: A growing hub for biotech companies and research institutions
- **Education**: Home to prestigious universities including UC San Diego and San Diego State University

## Culture and Lifestyle

The city celebrates its Mexican heritage and proximity to the border, evident in its cuisine, festivals, and vibrant Balboa Park, which houses numerous museums, gardens, and the famous zoo. San Diego Comic-Con, held annually, has become one of the world's largest pop culture events, drawing fans from across the globe.

With its combination of natural beauty, historical significance, and modern innovation, San Diego, California, continues to attract residents and visitors alike, solidifying its reputation as one of America's most desirable cities to live in and explore.

# The Myth of the Unassimilated Immigrant

By Ruben Navarrette Jr.

For as long as I've been writing about immigration — which is to say, for most of my adult life — I've heard the same lament from restrictionists: "Today's immigrants just don't assimilate like they used to."

It's a powerful narrative. It's also wrong.

I grew up in a Mexican American family in California's Central Valley, the descendant of people who crossed a border that crossed them first. I've spent decades covering immigration from the border to the Beltway, and I've watched this myth get recycled by every generation of nativists who conveniently forget that their own great-grandparents were once accused of the exact same crime: refusing to become American.

Now there's data to back up what those of us close to immigrant communities have always known. The Manhattan Institute, hardly a bastion of open-borders liberalism, released a study confirming that today's immigrants are assimilating at rates comparable to — and in some measures exceeding — those of the great waves of Ellis Island-era immigrants a century ago.

Let that sink in. A think tank known for rigorous, often conservative-leaning policy analysis looked at the data and concluded that the sky is not falling.

The study, which examined immigrants across generations using a comprehensive "assimilation index" measuring economic, cultural, and civic integration, found that immigrants who arrived in recent decades are learning English, marrying across ethnic lines, becoming citizens, and moving into the American mainstream at a pace that rivals or beats the Italians, Poles, and Jews who came through Ellis Island.

This should not surprise anyone who has actually spent time in immigrant communities rather than just theorizing about them from cable news green rooms.

Walk through any American city with a significant immigrant population and you'll see the same pattern that's repeated for over a century: the first generation struggles with English while working brutal jobs to give their kids a shot. The second generation is bilingual, straddling two worlds. By the third generation, the grandchildren often don't speak Spanish, or Tagalog, or Vietnamese at all — much to their grandparents' quiet heartbreak.

I've lived this. My own family's trajectory — from farmworkers to college graduates in three generations — is the assimilation story America has always told about itself, just with different surnames each time.

What's changed isn't the immigrants. It's us. We've developed collective amnesia about our own history. We forget that Benjamin Franklin once fretted that German immigrants in Pennsylvania would never assimilate and were "too swarthy" to be considered truly white. We forget that Italians were once considered an inferior, unassimilable race, subject to lynching in Louisiana. We forget the "No Irish Need Apply" signs.

Every generation of Americans looks at the newest arrivals and sees people who seem foreign, threatening, and resistant to American values — right up until those people's grandchildren are running for Congress, marrying into "old stock" American families, and blending seamlessly into the landscape.

The Manhattan Institute study also makes a point that critics of immigration conveniently ignore: modern communication technology, often blamed for helping immigrants maintain ties to their home countries and thus resist assimilation, hasn't actually slowed integration. Immigrants can call relatives in Guadalajara or Mumbai on WhatsApp and still enroll their kids in American schools, vote in American elections, and build American lives. Assimilation was never about severing all ties to the old country. It never has been.

None of this is to say there aren't real challenges — access to English classes, backlogs in citizenship processing, and communities that get concentrated enough that integration takes longer. These are policy problems worth solving. But they are not evidence of some fundamental refusal to assimilate. They're evidence that the system needs fixing, not that immigrants themselves are the problem.

What we're really talking about, when we talk about assimilation anxiety, is a discomfort with change itself — with hearing Spanish at the grocery store, with mosques going up next to churches, with the visible, audible evidence that America keeps being remade by the people who choose to come here.

That remaking has always been the point. It's not a bug in the American system. It's the feature that has kept this country dynamic, innovative, and relevant while older, more homogenous societies stagnate.

So the next time someone tells you immigrants today aren't assimilating like they used to, you now have the receipts. Send them the Manhattan Institute study. Then remind them that America has been having this same panic, with the same lack of evidence, for over 200 years.

We always come around. We always look back a generation later and wonder what the fuss was about. And the immigrants we once viewed with suspicion become, simply, Americans — the way immigrants always have.

# The Myth of the Unassimilating Immigrant

Every generation of Americans seems to rediscover the same anxiety: that this new wave of immigrants—unlike those who came before—simply refuses to become American.

Today, that suspicion falls on Latino and Asian immigrants. Critics point to Spanish-language signage, ethnic enclaves, and multigenerational households as evidence of a stubborn refusal to integrate. But this narrative isn't new. It's a script Americans have recycled for two centuries, and history reveals it was wrong every single time.

**The "Unassimilable" Irish**

In the 1850s, the Irish were considered a permanent underclass, incapable of true American citizenship. Political cartoons depicted them as apelike drunks. The Know-Nothing Party rose to national prominence on the promise of curbing Irish Catholic influence, warning that these immigrants owed allegiance to the Pope, not the Constitution. Irish enclaves in Boston and New York were seen as foreign colonies, not American neighborhoods.

Sound familiar?

**The German Threat**

By the late 19th century, German immigrants had created an extraordinary parallel society in America. German-language newspapers numbered in the hundreds. Entire school systems taught exclusively in German. Cities like Cincinnati and Milwaukee were functionally bilingual for decades. Nativists fretted that Germans would never truly become American—that their loyalty to Kaiser and Fatherland ran too deep.

**Italians and the "Racial" Question**

When Italian immigration surged around 1900, commentators didn't just doubt their capacity to assimilate—many didn't consider Italians "white" at all. They were portrayed as criminally inclined, clannish, and resistant to American individualism. The 1891 lynching of eleven Italian immigrants in New Orleans remains the largest mass lynching in American history, fueled by exactly these fears.

**What Actually Happened**

Assimilation wasn't a straight line—it was messy, generational, and often invisible in real time. First-generation immigrants clustered together, spoke their native languages, and maintained old-world customs. That's not resistance to America; it's simply how human beings navigate displacement. The magic happened in the second and third generations, as descendants of these "unassimilable" groups became senators, soldiers, and eventually indistinguishable markers of "real" Americans. JFK's election in 1960 was seen as proof Irish Catholics had finally arrived—a full century after their supposed unassimilability was declared.

**The Data Says the Same Story Is Unfolding**

Research consistently shows Latino and Asian immigrants are following nearly identical assimilation trajectories. English acquisition happens rapidly by the second generation. Intermarriage rates are high. Homeownership, educational attainment, and civic participation all increase substantially by the second and third generations—mirroring the patterns of Irish, German, and Italian assimilation.

The persistence of Spanish in some communities isn't fundamentally different from the persistence of German in 19th-century Wisconsin. It reflects immigration patterns and community formation, not a rejection of American identity.

**Why the Amnesia Matters**

We forget this history because assimilation, once complete, erases its own evidence. We don't remember that "Kennedy" was once a suspect name because eventually it wasn't. We don't recall German-only schoolhouses because German assimilated so successfully that few Americans today know their own ancestors once spoke it.

This selective memory allows each generation to view its own immigration anxieties as uniquely justified—as though this time, unlike all the previous times, the concerns are based on something real rather than the familiar discomfort of demographic change.

The question isn't whether Latino and Asian immigrants will assimilate. History suggests they already are, at rates consistent with every group that came before. The real question is whether Americans will recognize this pattern in time, or whether we'll need another fifty years of hindsight to admit we were wrong again.

# The Numbers Don't Lie: America's Immigrants Are Still Becoming American

There's a persistent anxiety in our national conversation that goes something like this: today's immigrants are different. Unlike the waves that came through Ellis Island, the story goes, modern immigrants are resistant to assimilation—content to live in linguistic enclaves, uninterested in American civic life, permanently separate from the mainstream.

It's a compelling narrative. It's also, according to rigorous data, largely wrong.

Economist Jacob Vigdor's Index of Immigrant Assimilation, produced under the auspices of the Manhattan Institute, offers one of the more careful empirical attempts to answer a simple question: are immigrants becoming American, and if so, how quickly? Vigdor's approach tracks assimilation across three distinct dimensions—economic, cultural, and civic—rather than treating "assimilation" as a single vague concept. The results complicate the pessimistic narrative considerably.

## The Economic Story: Convergence Over Time

On economic assimilation—measured through indicators like labor force participation, homeownership, and income convergence with native-born Americans—Vigdor's index finds a familiar and reassuring pattern. Immigrants generally arrive with an economic disadvantage relative to natives, but that gap narrows substantially with time spent in the country. The longer immigrants reside in the U.S., the more their economic profiles resemble those of native-born citizens.

This mirrors historical patterns going back a century. The first generation often struggles; economic parity tends to emerge over years and decades, not overnight. Critics who point to immigrant poverty rates as evidence of failed assimilation are often looking at a snapshot rather than a trajectory.

## Cultural Assimilation: Slower, But Real

The cultural dimension—centered heavily on English-language acquisition and intermarriage rates—is where Vigdor's findings get more interesting, and where public anxiety tends to concentrate. Here, the index suggests something worth taking seriously: cultural assimilation, by some measures, appears slower today than it was for earlier immigrant waves in the early twentieth century.

Part of this reflects simple demographics of proximity—large Spanish-speaking populations concentrated in certain regions can sustain linguistic communities in ways that dispersed European immigrant groups couldn't. But Vigdor's data doesn't support a story of stagnation so much as delayed convergence. English acquisition still occurs, particularly among the second generation, even if the first generation's pace looks different from that of Poles or Italians in 1910.

## Civic Assimilation: The Surprising Bright Spot

Perhaps the most underreported finding involves civic assimilation—naturalization rates, military service, and civic engagement. Here, contemporary immigrants often show civic integration that keeps pace with or exceeds historical patterns. Naturalization, in particular, remains a powerful marker: immigrants who take the step of becoming citizens are making a deliberate, often costly commitment to permanent membership in the American political community.

## What the Index Actually Tells Us

The value of Vigdor's work isn't that it resolves the immigration debate—it doesn't, and wasn't designed to. Its value lies in disaggregating "assimilation" into components that can be measured separately, revealing that the process isn't monolithic. Immigrants might integrate economically faster than culturally, or embrace civic participation while retaining linguistic ties to their country of origin.

This nuance matters for policy. If the concern is genuinely about assimilation—rather than immigration levels themselves—then policies should perhaps focus on the dimensions where convergence lags, such as English-language instruction, rather than treating all forms of integration as a single failing project.

The data suggests America's absorptive capacity, while not instantaneous, remains largely intact. That's a less dramatic headline than "immigrants aren't assimilating"—but it has the advantage of being true.

*[Note: This column presents a synthesized discussion of Vigdor's published research for illustrative purposes. Readers interested in the primary findings should consult the original Manhattan Institute reports for precise statistics and methodology.]*

counterfactuals.output:
# The Fields Remember Everything

I grew up in the Central Valley, where the fog rolls through almond orchards like it's got somewhere important to be, and where my grandmother's Spanish mixed with the Hmong, Punjabi, and Portuguese of neighbors who all somehow ended up in the same unlikely patch of California dirt. Fresno, Merced, Selma—these towns taught me something that no civics class ever could: assimilation, as we're told to understand it, is a myth built to make immigrants disappear rather than belong.

I remember the Hmong New Year celebrations at the fairgrounds every November, the way the parking lots overflowed and the air smelled like sausage and steamed rice cakes, the young women in their pomp and silver, the courtship ball-tossing games that looked like nothing else in America and everything like what a harvest festival should be—joyful, loud, unapologetically itself. And I remember, too, the letters to the editor. The complaints about "our town" not feeling like "our town" anymore. The same tired script, just aimed at different people than the ones aimed at my own family a generation before.

Here's what nobody wants to admit: assimilation was never really about learning English or paying taxes or loving apple pie. If it were, my grandfather—who worked the grape harvests for forty years, who paid every tax the government asked of him, who could recite baseball stats better than most gringos I know—would have been "assimilated" enough decades ago. But the goalposts always move. There's always some new marker of belonging just out of reach, because the myth isn't actually about culture. It's about control. It's about deciding who gets to be American without ever actually asking them to become anything.

The Hmong families who settled in the Valley after the Vietnam War and the CIA's secret war in Laos didn't come here by choice in any comfortable sense. They came because they'd fought and bled for American interests and then were left stateless when it was over. And when they got here, they did what every immigrant community does—they built something. Temples. Grocery stores. New Year celebrations that filled convention centers. They kept their language alive in the mouths of their children while those same children captained debate teams and enlisted in the Army and ran for city council. That's not resistance to assimilation. That's assimilation's actual definition, if we're honest about it: becoming American while remaining who you are, because who you are was never actually in conflict with being American in the first place.

But the backlash always comes anyway. I watched it happen to the Hmong community same as I'd watched it happen to Mexican families in Delano and Parlier a generation before. Someone always writes the letter. Someone always says the celebrations are "too loud" or the language on storefronts should be "in English first" or that these people "don't want to integrate." It's never true. It's never been true. What's actually happening is that Americans keep discovering, with theatrical surprise, that immigrants are exactly as complicated, industrious, foreign, familiar, and human as everyone else, and this discovery is treated each time like some kind of crisis.

My family didn't stop being Mexican to become American. We just became both, the way you become both a child and an adult, the way a language absorbs new words without ceasing to be itself. The Hmong families at that fairground weren't refusing America. They were adding to it, the way every group before them had, the way the Valley itself is made of a hundred small increments of arrival that somehow cohere into a whole.

The myth of assimilation demands a kind of disappearance—erase the accent, anglicize the name, stop cooking food that makes the neighbors curious, stop celebrating what makes you distinct—as if belonging requires vacancy. But I've never met an immigrant family that vanished. I've met families that multiplied what America was capable of holding. The Central Valley isn't less itself because of Hmong New Year or Mexican Independence Day parades or Punjabi gurdwaras humming with Sunday langar. It's more itself. It always was.

What the backlash really fears isn't a failure to assimilate. It's succeeding at something else entirely: proving that America was always supposed to be additive, not subtractive. That the fields, and the fog, and the towns built on immigrant labor were always going to keep remembering every person who came through, no matter how hard some tried to forget.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a CNN commentary piece titled something like "Immigrants assimilate faster than you think," debunking common myths about immigrant assimilation with historical and statistical evidence.
counterfactuals.output:
# Immigrants Assimilate Faster Than You Think

By the numbers, one of America's most persistent anxieties turns out to be one of its least justified.

For as long as immigrants have come to American shores, native-born citizens have worried they wouldn't fit in. Benjamin Franklin fretted that German immigrants in Pennsylvania would never learn English and would "Germanize us instead of us Anglifying them." A century later, it was the Irish and Italians who supposedly couldn't be absorbed into American life. Today, the same anxieties attach to immigrants from Latin America and Asia. The specifics change; the fear does not.

But decades of research from economists, historians, and demographers point to a consistent conclusion: today's immigrants are assimilating at rates comparable to—or faster than—those of a century ago.

## The English Language Myth

Perhaps no myth is more durable than the idea that today's immigrants, particularly Spanish speakers, aren't learning English. The data says otherwise.

According to Pew Research Center analysis, while only about 36% of first-generation Hispanic immigrants report speaking English very well, that number jumps to 89% among second-generation Hispanic Americans. By the third generation, English is overwhelmingly the dominant—and often only—language spoken at home. Spanish retention actually *declines* faster across generations than German or Italian did a century ago, according to research by Stanford sociologist Tomás Jiménez.

The pattern isn't new. Historical census data shows that most children of Italian and Polish immigrants in the early 20th century didn't speak their parents' native language fluently either. Assimilation into English has been the norm, not the exception, for over a century.

## Economic Integration Happens Within a Generation

Critics often point to the lower wages and educational attainment of recent immigrants as evidence of failed assimilation. But this confuses a snapshot with a trend.

Economic historians Leah Boustan and Ran Abramitzky, in their book "Streets of Gold," used millions of historical records to track immigrant families across generations. Their finding: children of poor immigrants—whether from Norway in 1910 or Mexico in 1980—consistently out-earn children of similarly poor U.S.-born parents. The economic mobility gap that seems so stark in the first generation narrows dramatically by the second.

This isn't a fluke of history. It holds true across sending countries and across a century of data. The son of a poor Mexican immigrant today is, statistically, more likely to climb the income ladder than the son of a poor U.S.-born citizen in the same town.

## Crime Rates Tell an Inconvenient Truth

The narrative linking immigration to crime has proven politically durable and empirically false. Study after study—including research from the libertarian Cato Institute, the National Academy of Sciences, and criminologists at the University of Wisconsin—finds that immigrants, including those undocumented, commit crimes at lower rates than native-born citizens.

A 2020 study published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences examined 150 years of census data and found no link between immigration and increased crime rates in any decade studied—including periods of the highest immigration in U.S. history. If anything, cities and neighborhoods with more immigrants tend to see *lower* crime rates, likely because immigrants have strong incentives to avoid legal trouble.

## Intermarriage: The Ultimate Assimilation Metric

Few things measure social integration as powerfully as who people choose to marry. By this metric, integration is happening quickly and thoroughly.

Pew data shows that about 39% of Asian American and 27% of Hispanic American newlyweds marry someone of a different racial or ethnic background—rates far higher than for Black or white Americans marrying outside their group. Intermarriage rates for Latino and Asian immigrants' children and grandchildren approach or exceed those recorded for European immigrant groups by the third generation in the early-to-mid 20th century.

## Civic Participation Follows a Familiar Arc

Naturalization rates, military service, and civic engagement all show similar patterns. Immigrants naturalize and vote at increasing rates the longer they reside in the U.S., and their children participate in civic life at rates comparable to other native-born Americans.

## Why the Myth Persists

If the evidence is so clear, why does the fear endure? Partly it's because assimilation is a generational process, and looking only at recent arrivals—rather than their children and grandchildren—creates a misleading snapshot. A newly arrived immigrant, by definition, hasn't had time to assimilate yet. That's not evidence of failure; it's evidence of the process working exactly as it always has.

Partly, too, it reflects a very human tendency to view one's own group's difficult integration story as the normal, patriotic one, while viewing the current wave with suspicion. Irish and Italian immigrants faced brutal discrimination and accusations of criminality and cultural incompatibility that sound remarkably similar to rhetoric used today about immigrants from Latin America or the Middle East.

## The Bottom Line

America has run this experiment before—repeatedly, with different groups, across more than a century. The results are remarkably consistent: immigrants and especially their children assimilate linguistically, economically, and socially in ways that mirror or exceed the patterns of earlier waves that Americans now celebrate as success stories.

The next time someone claims "these immigrants aren't like the ones who came before," it's worth remembering: that's exactly what people said about the ones who came before, too.

---

*Sources for this piece include research from the Pew Research Center, the National Academy of Sciences, the Cato Institute, and the book "Streets of Gold" by economists Ran Abramitzky and Leah Boustan.*
